official_ref: Minimum wage restoration ordinance, Lincoln City Council (adopted May 11, 2026)
plain_title: Keep yearly increases in Lincoln's $15 minimum wage
summary: In 2022, Nebraska voters said yes to a $15 minimum wage. Under that law, wages would rise a little each year to keep up with prices. In 2026, state lawmakers passed a new law. It caps that yearly rise at 1.75% and sets a lower wage for younger workers. This ordinance keeps the old rule for Lincoln instead. Wages here will keep rising with prices, not the new state cap.

impacts.text: Minimum-wage workers in Lincoln still get a raise each year based on prices. The state's new cap does not apply here.
This rule covers workers of every age. The state's lower wage for younger workers does not apply in Lincoln.

fiscal.text: No one has published a cost estimate for this ordinance. The cost is unknown.

votes_note: The ordinance passed 6-1. Available reporting did not publish how each council member voted by name.

official_ref: State ex rel. Hilgers v. Weber, Nebraska Supreme Court mandamus order (Sept. 9, 2026)
plain_title: Three citizen petitions to change city elections reach the ballot
summary: Three petitions asked Lincoln voters to change city elections. One would move city elections to even years, starting in 2028. One would limit council members to two terms in a row. One would let some people who live just outside the city vote in city elections, but not on bond questions. Organizers collected enough signatures for all three. The city said the petitions came in too late for the November 2026 ballot. The Nebraska Supreme Court disagreed. It ordered the city to put all three on this November's ballot. On September 14, 2026, the mayor and council chair proposed their own versions of two of the changes.

impacts.text: If this passes, Lincoln's next city election moves from 2027 to 2028. That lines up with state and federal elections.
If this passes, council members can serve at most two four-year terms in a row.
If this passes, some people who live near Lincoln but not inside it could vote in city elections. They could not vote on bond questions.

votes_note: This wasn't decided by a council vote. Organizers gathered petition signatures, and the Nebraska Supreme Court ordered the city to put the measures on the ballot.

official_ref: Nebraska State Auditor report OE550201-12142023 (Lincoln Airport Authority / Red Way)
plain_title: Airport board's $700,000 bet on an airline that failed
summary: The Lincoln Airport Authority is a 5-member board. Lincoln voters elect this board separately from the city council. In 2022 and 2023, the board backed a new airline called Red Way. It gave the airline federal pandemic-relief money. It also waived fees the airline owed. Red Way stopped flying after less than three months, in August 2023. A state audit found the board spent more than $700,000 in local public money on the deal. The audit said the deal broke state law.

impacts.text: The board promised up to $3 million in federal pandemic-relief money to help Red Way start flying.
The board gave more than $700,000 in local public money. It also waived fees Red Way owed.
Red Way expected $8.8 million in ticket sales in its first three months. It sold about a quarter of that.

fiscal.text: The audit found more than $700,000 in local public money spent on this deal. Counting waived fees and federal money, the total may be near $3.7 million.

board_note: These are the Authority's current elected board members. Available reporting did not confirm the board's exact makeup at the time the Red Way deal was approved.
votes_note: The Lincoln Airport Authority is a separate elected board. Your city council member does not vote on its decisions.

official_ref: 2024 Stormwater and Flood Management Bond, approved by voters Nov. 5, 2024
plain_title: A $13.9 million bond to fix flooding and drainage citywide
summary: Lincoln's stormwater system needs regular fixes. These fixes cut flooding and improve water quality. In July 2024, the city council voted to ask voters for a bond. The bond is $13.9 million over 20 years. It pays for more than 20 drainage and flood-control projects. Voters approved the bond in November 2024. Lincoln has passed bonds like this before.

impacts.text: The bond costs the average Lincoln home about $9.65 a year. That home is worth about $280,000. The extra cost starts in the 2025-26 tax year.
About $5.7 million goes to drainage studies and projects. About $3.6 million goes to flood reduction. Another $3.6 million goes to stream work. $1 million goes to water quality and street sweepers.
Some of the projects are at 48th and Cornhusker, 10th and Park Avenue, and Haines Branch.

fiscal.text: Total bond: $13.9 million over 20 years. It costs the average homeowner about $9.65 a year.

plain_title: Nebraska Medicaid to pay for at-home nurse visits
summary: Nebraska already funds some home-visiting programs for new parents. This law adds a new way to pay for one kind: nurse visits for postpartum mothers and babies six months old or younger. It only covers families on Medicaid. The state must ask the federal government to approve the change by October 2025. Families can say no to a visit at any time.

impacts.text: Medicaid families with a baby six months old or younger can get visits from a nurse at home. They can turn down a visit at any time.
The state plans to pay its share from a specific health-care fund, not general tax money. If that fund runs short, lawmakers may need to find money elsewhere.
The state's own estimate puts the cost at about $1.1 million in the first year and about $2.2 million the year after. Most of that is paid back by federal Medicaid money.

fiscal.text: State fiscal analysts estimate $1,075,600 in year one ($601,691 federal, $473,909 from a state health-care fund) and $2,151,200 in year two ($1,177,997 federal, $973,203 state).

votes_note: The bill passed 47-0, with 2 present but not voting, on Final Reading. Individual votes by name were not confirmed for this card.
